newsitem.title: INDIA: India gold prices seen staying lower.
newsitem.headline: India gold prices seen staying lower.

text.p: Gold prices in the Indian subcontinent are seen staying lower this week due to higher supplies in India and a weakening rupee that has eased demand for Dubai-based gold, investors and dealers said on Monday.
The exception was Pakistan, where prices were set to rise after a two-week fall. Higher demand would flow from good cotton and rice crops boosting growers' coffers, they said.

Dealers in Bombay, India's commercial capital, said there was some support last week due to festival buying at lower levels. "If the festival demand was not there, the market would have fallen further," one said.
The Customs department, which occasionally releases into the market previously seized smuggled gold, said prices were not yet high enough to release its stock of 250-300 gold biscuits.
"If prices in the open market go up to attractive levels we will start selling," customs officer R.S. Sawant said.
Gold prices in Bombay fell by 10 rupees per 10 grammes to 5,170 rupees in the week to Monday. Gold biscuits (116.50 grammes) eased by 140 rupees at 60,500 rupees a piece in the same period.
Dealers in Pakistan's commercial centre of Karachi said on Monday that gold rates were seen rising due to higher demand from jewellers in Punjab.
Another factor that could increase gold rates is the likely lower adjustment of the rupee against the dollar, dealer Saeed Qureshi said. "The rupee's depreciation will push gold rates up."
Dealer Fahim Hamid Ali said gold demand was rising in Punjab, which produces most of the country's cotton and rice, because of growers' expected higher income from good crops.
Prices in Pakistan rose slightly in the week to Sunday after easing earlier due to floods in some areas and a weak rupee.
Traders in Dubai, the main feeder market into India and which is the world's single largest gold market, said a weaker rupee had capped Indian demand for gold from the Gulf Arab emirate.

Though demand into India and Pakistan remains upbeat after the end of monsoon rains, subcontinent importers face higher costs because of the depreciation of the Indian rupee against the dollar and a narrow trading arbitrage from Dubai to Bombay, traders said.

"The bearish trend in the international market will not be of much help to the Indian gold and silver demand as the Indian rupee is trending lower," said Sultan Satani at Dubai-based Satco Global Trading.
The Indian rupee was quoted at 35.69 to the dollar at midday on Monday, down from 35.45 on September 1 close.
"It will continue to keep prices on the high side," one Dubai trader said.
